steps.action: Pose the aim of linking tectonically quiescent river incision to carbon export and CO2 drawdown across the 2.6 and 1 Ma climate changes.
steps.quote: to elucidate links among tectonically quiescent river incision, carbon export, and atmospheric CO 2 drawdown

steps.action: Take from the authors' earlier Fortymile River work two terrace levels whose incision pulses are synchronous with Bering Sea sedimentation changes.
steps.quote: synchronous with pulses of continental river incision archived in two well-preserved strath terrace levels (T1 and T2)

steps.action: Adopt from published work the hypothesis that tributary incision was forced by climate, indirectly through ice-sheet river capture at 2.6 Ma and directly through Middle Pleistocene runoff at 1 Ma.
steps.quote: attesting to widespread river incision likely forced by latest Cenozoic climate change

steps.action: Select the central Yukon basin as a found setting with tectonic quiescence and uniform crystalline bedrock, so that incision is sensitive to climate rather than uplift.
steps.quote: define a tectonically quiescent late Cenozoic erosional system more sensitive to climate than rock uplift or erodibility

steps.action: Design the Charley River sampling to match the Fortymile chronology: three T1 sites test whether ages decrease upstream, and one T2 site tests for a Middle Pleistocene transition age.
steps.quote: We designed our sample strategy to directly compare results with the previously developed Fortymile River terrace chronology

steps.action: Map terraces T1 and T2, the channel, and a periglacial pediment on the IfSAR DEM; measure tread heights in the field; collect quartz samples; measure 26Al and 10Be by AMS at Purdue.
steps.quote: We mapped high and intermediate terrace levels (T1 and T2, respectively) and the Charley River channel

steps.action: Fit 26Al/10Be burial isochrons with the Zhao et al. (2016) linearization, giving T1 ages of 2.2, 1.8 and 1.6 Ma decreasing upstream and a T2 age of 1.1 Ma.
steps.quote: decrease upstream on high terrace T1 from 2.2 ± 0.3 Ma near the Yukon–Charley River confluence

steps.action: Correct each measurement for blank backgrounds and screen the isochron fits for outliers; all 19 samples fall within 2 sigma, so none is omitted.
steps.quote: All 19 of the isotope concentration pairs plotted within 2 σ of the regression lines

steps.action: Infer from the terrace height-age data that incision propagated about 140 km upstream at about 160 mm/kyr, stalled from 1.6 to 1.1 Ma, and resumed at 1.1 Ma.
steps.quote: Charley River incision propagated ∼ 140 km upstream at ∼ 160 mm kyr - 1 from 2.2 to 1.6 Ma

steps.action: Compare the new Charley chronology with the independent Fortymile, Klondike and Birch Creek terrace records, which show matching incision onset and stall timing.
steps.quote: Our Charley River incision chronology closely matches previously established Fortymile (Bender et al., 2020), Klondike River

steps.action: Retain the claim of climate-modulated regional incision pulses: an ice-sheet-triggered wave from 2.6 Ma and Middle Pleistocene transition resumption at 1.1 Ma.
steps.quote: these terrace chronologies demonstrate climate-modulated pulses of central Yukon River incision that disrupt regional aggradation

steps.action: Combine published U1341 age-depth data into a five-segment OLS age-depth model, derive linear sedimentation rates, and convert constituent depths to ages.
steps.quote: fit ordinary least squares regression models to each segment

steps.action: Check that the revised age-depth model closely matches the independent Horikawa et al. (2015) model.
steps.quote: to modestly revise an age–depth model that closely matches that of Horikawa et al. (2015)

steps.action: Estimate the organic-matter source from C/N endmembers (about 85% marine) and compute TOC and Si_xs mass accumulation rates with propagated LSR and density uncertainties.
steps.quote: imply organic matter predominantly ( ∼ 85 %) derived from marine NEP

steps.action: Compare the incision pulses with Bering Sea records: at 2.6-2.1 Ma, provenance shifts toward Yukon sources, sedimentation triples, and TOC and Si_xs accumulation rise 2-4 fold (Figure 4, p. 1047).
steps.quote: Synchronous with the initial incision pulse, from 2.6–2.1 Ma Bering Sea sediment

steps.action: Name the published rival, North Pacific nutrient leakage as the driver of the productivity increase, and offer Yukon incision as an alternative explanation, using provenance proxies.
steps.quote: the prior interpretations of North Pacific nutrient leakage as a driver of increased Si x s MAR

steps.action: Compare the second incision pulse with Bering Sea records: sedimentation doubles at 1.1-0.8 Ma with increased continentality and doubled TOC and Si_xs accumulation.
steps.quote: the rate of Bering Sea sedimentation doubled between 1.1 and 0.8 Ma

steps.action: Retain the claim that Yukon incision increased Bering Sea carbon sequestration through terrestrial carbon burial and boosted marine NEP.
steps.quote: Consistent timing among these records strongly suggests that Yukon River incision and sediment export increased Bering Sea carbon sequestration

steps.action: Check the mixed-source organic carbon interpretation against independent C/N ratios at shelf site U1343.
steps.quote: consistent with our C / N ratio-based interpretation of mixed terrestrial and marine organic sediment sources

steps.action: Compare the two pulses with published boron-isotope and alkenone pCO2 reconstructions: over 100 ppm decrease at about 2.4 Ma, and a 25-30 ppm dip in some records at the second pulse.
steps.quote: both the maximum and range of atmospheric p CO 2 reconstructed from δ 11 B

steps.action: Propose that fluvial-erosion carbon burial and NEP in river systems worldwide may have contributed to late Cenozoic pCO2 drawdown.
steps.quote: Decreased p CO 2 during these late Cenozoic climate changes may reflect enhanced terrestrial carbon burial and marine NEP

steps.action: Conclude that incision across more than 60,000 km2 at 2.6 and 1.1 Ma controlled terrigenous carbon and nutrient export and Bering Sea sequestration.
steps.quote: This coupling strongly suggests that Yukon River incision controlled terrigenous organic carbon and nutrient export to the Bering Sea

end.claim: Climate-forced pulses of central Yukon River incision at about 2.6 and 1.1 Ma controlled terrigenous organic carbon and nutrient export to the Bering Sea, raising carbon sequestration via burial and marine net export production.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the timing comparison of the tributary incision chronologies against the U1341 provenance, sedimentation-rate and TOC/Si_xs accumulation records, there would be no coupling claim.

gates.evidence: The sampling design was directed by expectations from the Fortymile chronology: 'to test whether the terrace age decreases upstream' and to see if T2 dates to the Middle Pleistocene transition (§3.2 ¶2). The Bering Sea data were all pre-existing and compiled after the fact. The Charley ages could have failed to match the other tributaries, and the timing could have mismatched the cores, but the rival (nutrient leakage) was not tested against distinct predictions. The design aims were plausibly fixed before sampling (inference), but no registration is documented.

limits: No peer-review file or open discussion was supplied, although the paper went through ESurf Discussion with two named referees (Hage, Zondervan), so changes during review cannot be coded. Age-depth segments were 'visually identified'; no sensitivity test of segmentation, density assumption, or weight-percent uncertainty is reported. The coupling rests on coincident timing; the nutrient-leakage rival is offered an 'alternative explanation' but not excluded by a distinct prediction (inference). The organic source fraction is ambiguous: about 85% marine with one endmember, about 86% terrigenous with the Yukon endmember. The conclusion reports '~85% marine' without resolving this. A sentence in §4.4 ¶1 appears truncated in the source. Sub-claims: Charley River burial ages and incision rates are estimate_with_resolution; regional incision pulses across four tributaries are best_explanation, close to regularity_in_range; the global pCO2 contribution is a hypothesis with status none.

disagreements.target: Long-debated position that enhanced silicate weathering consumed enough CO2 to amplify global cooling (Hilton and West, 2020)
disagreements.support: Cited work shows silicate weathering is limited at high erosion rates and that sedimentary-rock denudation raises pCO2, so a weathering-independent sequestration mechanism is needed.
disagreements.quote: However, silicate weathering is subordinate to physical erosion only at low erosion rates (West et al., 2005)
